name: JavaScript
description: Coercion, closures, the event loop, prototypes and the modern language features that replaced the old workarounds.

modules.name: Semantics & Coercion
modules.description: Types, equality, scoping and the behaviours JavaScript is famous for.

cards.answer: `==` coerces operands to a common type before comparing; `===` compares type and value with no coercion.

left.title: == (loose)
points: `null == undefined` is true (the one useful case)
Non-transitive in places — hard to reason about

right.title: === (strict)
points: The default choice in every style guide

cards.explanation: Use `===` everywhere except the idiom `x == null`, which tests for null or undefined in one go. For NaN use `Number.isNaN`; for the SameValue semantics that distinguish -0 use `Object.is`.

`var` declarations are hoisted and initialised to `undefined`. `let`/`const` are hoisted too, but sit in the temporal dead zone until the declaration executes — touching them first throws a ReferenceError. That is a feature: it turns a silent bug into a loud one.

cards.prompt: What determines the value of `this` in a JavaScript function?
cards.answer: The call site, in this precedence: `new` binding → explicit `call`/`apply`/`bind` → method call (the object before the dot) → default (undefined in strict mode, globalThis otherwise). Arrow functions ignore all of it and inherit `this` lexically.
cards.explanation: `this` is not the defining scope — it is decided when the function is invoked. `const f = obj.method; f()` loses the receiver. Arrow functions have no `this` of their own, which is exactly why they are the right choice for callbacks inside methods.

`var` is function-scoped, so all three closures share one binding that ends at 3. `let` creates a fresh binding per iteration — the loop head is re-bound each pass — so each closure captures its own value.

cards.prompt: How does property lookup work on a JavaScript object?
cards.answer: The engine checks the object's own properties, then walks `[[Prototype]]` (`Object.getPrototypeOf`) link by link until it finds the key or reaches null.
cards.explanation: `class` is syntax over this: methods live on `Ctor.prototype`, and every instance links to it. This is why adding a method to a prototype affects existing instances, and why shadowing a prototype property with an own property hides it rather than overwriting it.

resources.title: MDN — Inheritance and the prototype chain

cards.prompt: Why does mutating the copy still change the original?
cards.answer: Spread is a **shallow** copy — `copy.tags` is the same array reference. Deep-clone with `structuredClone(original)` or copy nested values explicitly.
cards.explanation: `{...o}` and `Object.assign({}, o)` copy one level of own enumerable properties. Any nested object or array is shared. `structuredClone` handles most structures (not functions or DOM nodes) and is built into modern runtimes.

cards.prompt: `a?.b` returns undefined instead of throwing when `a` is null or ___.
cards.explanation: Optional chaining short-circuits on exactly two values: `null` and `undefined`. It pairs with `??` (nullish coalescing), which falls back only on those same two values — unlike `||`, which also fires on `0`, `''` and `false`.

modules.name: The Event Loop & Async
modules.description: Tasks, microtasks, promises and the ordering rules that decide when your code runs.

cards.prompt: What does this print, and why in that order?
cards.explanation: Synchronous code runs first (1, 4). Then the **microtask** queue drains completely — promise callbacks (3). Only then does the event loop take the next **macrotask**, the timer callback (2). Microtasks always beat timers, no matter the delay.

cards.prompt: This takes 10 seconds instead of 1. Why, and how do you fix it?
cards.answer: `await` inside the loop serialises the requests. Start them all first and await together: `await Promise.all(urls.map(u => fetch(u)))`.
cards.explanation: Sequential await is correct when each request depends on the previous one, and wasteful otherwise. Use `Promise.all` for fail-fast parallelism, `Promise.allSettled` when partial failure is acceptable, and a concurrency limiter when the target has rate limits.

cards.prompt: What are the states of a Promise, and which transitions are legal?
cards.answer: Pending → fulfilled (with a value) or rejected (with a reason). Settlement is permanent — a promise can never change state again or settle twice.
cards.explanation: That immutability is what makes promises composable: attaching `.then` after settlement still fires, and the value cannot be retracted. An unhandled rejection is a warning in browsers and, by default, a fatal error in modern Node.

cards.answer: `forEach` ignores the returned promises, so the async callbacks run detached — their rejections become unhandled rejections outside the try block. Use `for...of` with `await`, or `await Promise.all(items.map(...))`.
cards.explanation: `try/catch` only catches synchronous throws in its own frame. An async callback returns a promise immediately; the throw happens later, on a different tick, with nobody listening. Array methods other than `map` have no idea what a promise is.

cards.answer: Debounce waits for silence before firing once; throttle fires at most once per interval during activity.

left.title: Debounce
points: Resets a timer on every event
Can starve forever under constant input

right.title: Throttle
points: Fires at a fixed maximum rate

cards.explanation: Ask what the user should see: nothing until they pause (debounce) or steady updates while they act (throttle). Getting this backwards is a common source of janky or unresponsive UI.

modules.name: Modern JavaScript & Runtime
modules.description: Modules, iteration protocols, memory and the runtime facts behind everyday code.

cards.answer: ESM is static, asynchronous and live-bound; CommonJS is dynamic, synchronous and value-copied.

left.title: ESM (import/export)
points: Live bindings: importer sees later mutations

right.title: CJS (require/module.exports)
points: Resolved at runtime, can be conditional
Copies the value at require time

cards.explanation: The static structure is the whole point: bundlers can only tree-shake and split what they can see without running your code. Mixing them (`require` of ESM) is where most Node packaging pain comes from.

cards.prompt: What makes an object usable with `for...of` and spread?
cards.answer: A `[Symbol.iterator]()` method returning an iterator — an object with `next()` that yields `{ value, done }`. Generator functions produce one for free.
cards.explanation: `for...of`, spread, destructuring, `Array.from`, `Promise.all` and `yield*` all speak this protocol. Implementing it makes a custom collection behave like a built-in. `for...in`, by contrast, walks enumerable string keys including inherited ones — rarely what you want.

cards.prompt: `Map` vs plain object as a dictionary
cards.answer: Map takes any key type, preserves insertion order, has `size`, and has no prototype keys to collide with.

left.title: Map
points: Keys of any type, including objects

cards.explanation: Use a Map for a real keyed collection that grows at runtime, an object for a struct with known fields. `Object.create(null)` removes the prototype hazard if you must use an object as a dictionary.

Every JS number is an IEEE-754 double. 0.1 and 0.2 are not exactly representable in binary, so their sum is not exactly 0.3. Past 2^53 the gap between representable integers is 2, so `MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 2` rounds back to 9007199254740992 — the same value as `MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 1`. Use `BigInt` for exact large integers and integer cents for money.

cards.prompt: A single-page app grows to 2 GB after an hour of navigation. What are the usual suspects?
cards.answer: Listeners and timers never removed, detached DOM nodes still referenced by JS, unbounded caches/arrays, and closures capturing large objects.
cards.explanation: GC frees only unreachable objects. An `addEventListener` on `window`, an `setInterval`, or a module-level array holds references forever. Fix by removing listeners on teardown (AbortController signals make this one line), clearing timers, and bounding caches — `WeakMap`/`WeakRef` where the key's lifetime should drive the entry's.
